newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean Hanbo founder faces arrest.
newsitem.headline: South Korean Hanbo founder faces arrest.

text.p: A South Korean court on Friday issued an arrest warrant for the founder of the troubled Hanbo Group over a loan scandal, while the government began steps to rescue the conglomerate's steelmaking flagship.
"The court granted our request for the arrest warrant for Chung Tae-soo," a prosecution official told Reuters. "Mr Chung will be arrested later today and taken to a Seoul prison."
Prosecutors summoned Chung from a Seoul hospital on Thursday and have since questioned him over massive loans to financially shaky Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's 14th largest conglomerate.

Choi Byung-koog, head of the prosecution's Central Investigation Department, told reporters that Chung would be initially charged with illegally issuing cheques and violating the law on mutual trust and savings companies.
"All suspicions and allegations about him could be investigated once he is arrested," he said.

A prosecution source said investigators had found out that Chung had illegally issued hundreds of millions of dollars worth of cheques and illegally withdrew loans from the Hanbo Group's trust and savings unit.
"But the main focus of investigation would be on loans from Hanbo Steel's creditor banks," he said. "Chung will also be questioned if he bribed anybody to secure the loans."
Chung has never commented on any charges of wrongdoing.
Hanbo Steel, the nation's second largest steelmaker, defaulted on debt repayments last week after piling up five trillion won ($5.8 billion) in loans from 61 banks and financial institutions.
Government officials said although Chung must face justice for any illegal activity, the steel company would be rescued to control the shock to the economy.

Finance and Economy Minister Han Seung-soo reported to President Kim Young-sam that about 100 billion won would be set aside to keep Hanbo Steel running and to help the company's suppliers weather Hanbo's problems.
At a meeting between Kim and his top economic officials, Han said the emergency fund would help Hanbo pay for raw materials and transport costs, according to ministry officials.
The fund would also be used to pay wages of workers at Hanbo's suppliers and subcontractors.

Kim said Hanbo's failure, which followed nearly a month of nationwide labour strife, posed further difficulties to the already slowing economy and that the government should make sure Hanbo Steel keeps operating, his spokesman said.

"Steps should be taken to aid smooth production at Hanbo Steel plants which are already operational," Kim said. "A fair assessment must be made of the mill under construction and it should be completed as scheduled if it proves to be feasible."
Han said a buyer could be found once Hanbo Steel finished building its new mill, which has an annual capacity of six million tonnes, later this year.

Hanbo Steel and three affiliates are awaiting court rulings on their applications for receivership. A Seoul court said on Friday it had decided to freeze Hanbo Steel assets until a decision was made on the receivership.

Hanbo's creditors have said they will support receivership by suspending demands for debt repayments. They said they would reopen overdraft facilities with the insolvent company from Saturday or Monday.
President Kim, who ordered a thorough probe into the loans on Monday, said the crisis appeared to stem from Hanbo Steel's heavy reliance on borrowing to fund excessive expansion.

Chung acquired or set up 18 firms in the past three years. He had been admitted to hospital after complaining of high blood pressure on Tuesday but doctors said his health was relatively sound. ($1 = 861 won)
